docs.text: A filesystem you can replace in a test ¶ The problem ¶ std::filesystem is a set of free functions. Code that calls them talks to the real disk, and there is no place to put anything between the code and the disk. bool has_config(const std::filesystem::path& dir) { return std::filesystem::is_regular_file(dir / "config.txt"); } A test of this function needs a real directory with a real file. That has a price: Tests touch the disk. They need a temporary directory, clean-up, and care about parallel runs. Failures are hard to make. To test "permission denied" or "disk is full" you must arrange them on a real machine. Errors are everywhere. Most functions throw std::filesystem::filesystem_error , and every function has a second overload with std::error_code . Each call site picks one of two styles and repeats it. No view of the calls. You cannot ask "which paths did this code touch?" without a debugger. The bytes of a file are not covered. std::filesystem knows about files, but not about reading or writing them. The code that reads a file uses std::ifstream , which is another thing a test cannot replace. What the library does ¶ virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t is a struct. Every member is a std::function , and every member is one operation that a filesystem must answer: status , file_size , rename , list , read , write and so on. Production code takes a const filesystem_t& and calls its members: bool has_config( const virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t& filesystem, const virtual_filesystem::path_t& dir ) { return virtual_filesystem::is_regular_file(filesystem, dir / "config.txt"); } In the program the filesystem is made from std::filesystem : const auto filesystem = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({}); In a test any member is replaced by a function that answers what the test needs: virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t&) { return std::filesystem::file_status{std::filesystem::file_type::regular}; }; What you get: A seam. The code under test sees filesystem_t and does not know what is behind it. A fake per member. A test sets only the members the code under test calls. One error policy. make_filesystem catches filesystem_error and hands it to one function, on_error . The call does not throw unless that function does. A log of calls. A logger function sees every call, with its paths, before it runs. Rules that cannot disagree with a fake. exists , is_directory , is_empty , relative and the other queries are free functions built on the members. A fake status changes what they answer. File bytes. try_read , read and write are members too, and a content_filter can change the bytes on the way in and out. It is a thin layer. It adds no files and no state of its own: make_filesystem forwards each call to std::filesystem . How this documentation is arranged ¶ Getting started : requirements, CMake and a first program. The guide: Replacing calls in a test : fakes, partial fakes and failing fakes. Errors and logging : logger , on_error and the value you get back. Queries : the rules built on the members. Listing a directory : list and its options. File bytes and content_filter : try_read , read , write and the filter. Reference : every function, type and enumeration.

docs.text:
File bytes and content_filter ¶ std::filesystem knows about files, not about their contents. The code that reads a file uses std::ifstream , and a test cannot replace that. So filesystem_t has three members for the bytes of a file, and one function that can change the bytes on the way. using bytes_t = std::string; using bytes_ot = std::optional<bytes_t>; using try_read_ft = std::function<bytes_ot (const path_t&)>; using read_ft = std::function<bytes_t (const path_t&)>; using write_ft = std::function<void (const write_t&)>; struct write_t { path_t path; bytes_t bytes; }; The bytes are a std::string . The files are opened in binary mode, so nothing is translated. try_read, read and write ¶ member does try_read(path) returns the bytes, or an empty optional when the file cannot be opened. That is not an error : on_error does not run read(path) returns the bytes. When the file cannot be opened it is an error: filesystem_error goes to on_error write({.path, .bytes}) replaces the bytes of the file. The file is created, or truncated if it exists Use try_read when a missing file is normal, for example an optional config. Use read when a missing file is a failure. // the text of dir/config.txt, or an empty string when there is none filesystem.try_read(dir / "config.txt").value_or(""); An empty optional is different from an empty file: an empty file is bytes_ot{""} . content_filter ¶ content_filter is a function that gets the bytes on their way in and out of the filesystem and returns the bytes to use instead: enum class content_filter_direction_et { READ, WRITE }; using content_filter_ft = std::function<bytes_t ( const path_t&, const bytes_t&, content_filter_direction_et )>; The arguments are the path, the bytes, and the direction: direction the bytes are the result is READ what the filesystem read from the file what read or try_read returns WRITE what the caller gave to write what the filesystem writes to the file Use it for what must happen to every file: decoding, decrypting, converting line endings, removing a byte order mark. The code that calls read and write does not change. An empty content_filter leaves the bytes as they are. With make_filesystem ¶ Pass the filter to make_filesystem . It is applied to try_read , read and write before the filesystem is returned. This filter shifts every byte up by one on the way to the disk and down on the way back. The shift is a stand-in for real encryption: const auto filesystem = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({ .content_filter = []( const virtual_filesystem::path_t&, const virtual_filesystem::bytes_t& bytes, const virtual_filesystem::content_filter_direction_et direction ) { const auto shift = direction == virtual_filesystem::content_filter_direction_et::WRITE ? 1 : -1; auto result = bytes; std::ranges::transform(result, result.begin(), [shift](const char c) { return static_cast<char>(c + shift); }); return result; } }); filesystem.write({.path = file, .bytes = "HAL"}); filesystem.read(file); // "HAL" filesystem.try_read(file); // "HAL" A filesystem without the filter sees what is on the disk: const auto plain = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({}); plain.read(file); // "IBM" With a filesystem you built ¶ A filesystem_t that you filled by hand, for a test, has its content_filter set but not applied. Call apply_content_filter once. It wraps the three members of the filesystem: void apply_content_filter(filesystem_t&); virtual_filesystem::bytes_t on_disk = "one
two
"; virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.read = [&](const virtual_filesystem::path_t&) { return on_disk; }; filesystem.write = [&](const virtual_filesystem::write_t& args) { on_disk = args.bytes; }; filesystem.content_filter = []( const virtual_filesystem::path_t&, const virtual_filesystem::bytes_t& bytes, const virtual_filesystem::content_filter_direction_et direction ) { if (direction == virtual_filesystem::content_filter_direction_et::WRITE) { return bytes; } auto text = bytes; std::erase(text, ''); return text; }; virtual_filesystem::apply_content_filter(filesystem); filesystem.read("notes.txt"); // "one
two
": the carriage returns are gone The test checks the filter without any file: the fake read returns what the "disk" holds, and the filter turns it into what the code sees. Warning apply_content_filter wraps what the members are at the moment of the call. Call it once. A second call wraps the wrapped members, and the filter runs twice. make_filesystem already calls it, so do not call it again on its result. Details ¶ try_read calls the filter only when it has bytes . A missing file stays an empty optional and the filter is not called. The filter wraps the members from the outside. An exception from the filter leaves the call; on_error does not see it. If read fails and on_error returns, read returns empty bytes and the filter is called with them. The filter sees every file the same way. Look at the path when files differ. The logger sees TRY_READ , READ and WRITE . The filter is not a call of its own and is not logged.

docs.text: Errors and logging ¶ make_filesystem fills a filesystem_t from std::filesystem and puts two functions around every call: a logger that runs before the call, and an error handler that receives a std::filesystem::filesystem_error . struct make_filesystem_t { logger_ft logger; // void (const log_t&) error_ft on_error; // void (const std::filesystem::filesystem_error&) content_filter_ft content_filter; // see "File bytes and content_filter" }; filesystem_t make_filesystem(const make_filesystem_t&); Every field is optional. An empty function is skipped. The order of events ¶ For every call the order is the same: The logger runs with a log_t : which operation, which paths. The call goes to std::filesystem . If std::filesystem throws filesystem_error , on_error runs with it. std::vector<std::string> events; const auto filesystem = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({ .logger = [&](const virtual_filesystem::log_t& log) { events.push_back("log " + log.path.generic_string()); }, .on_error = [&](const std::filesystem::filesystem_error& error) { events.push_back("error " + error.path1().generic_string()); } }); filesystem.file_size("missing.txt"); filesystem.rename({.from = "missing_a.txt", .to = "missing_b.txt"}); events is now: log missing.txt error missing.txt log missing_a.txt error missing_a.txt A call is logged even when it fails, and a call that does not fail is logged and nothing more. What the call returns when on_error returns ¶ filesystem_error does not leave the call. When on_error returns, the call returns a value-initialized result , the same as Result{} : the call returns after an error bool ( create_directory , remove , equivalent , ...) false std::uintmax_t ( file_size , remove_all , ...) 0 path_t ( canonical , read_symlink , ...) an empty path fs::file_status ( status , symlink_status ) type none fs::file_time_type the epoch of the clock fs::space_info all three sizes 0 entries_t ( list ) no entries bytes_t ( read ) no bytes bytes_ot ( try_read ) an empty optional void ( rename , write , ...) nothing const auto filesystem = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({}); filesystem.file_size("missing.txt"); // 0 filesystem.read_symlink("missing.txt"); // an empty path filesystem.list({.root = "missing_dir"}); // no entries filesystem.read("missing.txt"); // no bytes filesystem.remove("missing.txt"); // false Here the filesystem has no on_error at all: the call neither logs nor throws, and the result is empty. That is the way to say "I do not care about errors". Warning A result that is empty after an error looks like a result that is empty because there is nothing to find. If the difference matters, record the error in on_error , or make on_error throw. exists , is_directory and the other queries treat a status of type none like not_found : a file that could not be examined is not there. What is not an error ¶ Some calls fail without filesystem_error , because std::filesystem and the library say so: status and symlink_status of a missing file return file_type::not_found . on_error does not run. try_read of a file that cannot be opened returns an empty optional. on_error does not run. That is why the function exists next to read . read of a file that cannot be opened is an error: it throws filesystem_error with no_such_file_or_directory for a missing file and io_error for another reason, so on_error runs. write that cannot open or finish the file is an error with io_error . An exception from on_error ¶ on_error may throw an exception of its own. The library does not catch it: it leaves the call. Use it to turn a filesystem_error into your own type, or to stop at the first failure: const auto strict = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({ .on_error = [](const std::filesystem::filesystem_error& error) { throw std::runtime_error{"cannot use " + error.path1().filename().string()}; } }); strict.file_size("missing.txt"); // throws std::runtime_error "cannot use missing.txt" The same holds for the logger: an exception from it leaves the call, and the call to std::filesystem is not made. The log ¶ struct log_t { operation_et operation; path_t path; path_t other; }; operation is one of the values of operation_et : STATUS , FILE_SIZE , RENAME , LIST , READ , WRITE and so on. There is one value for every member of filesystem_t except content_filter . path is the file the call names. It is empty for calls that name no path: CURRENT_PATH and TEMP_DIRECTORY . other is the second path of a call that names two: the target of RENAME , COPY , CREATE_SYMLINK , CREATE_DIRECTORY_SYMLINK and CREATE_HARD_LINK , and the second path of EQUIVALENT . It is empty for all the others. const auto filesystem = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({ .logger = [](const virtual_filesystem::log_t& log) { std::cout << log.path.generic_string() << " -> " << log.other.generic_string() << "\n"; } }); filesystem.rename({.from = "missing_a.txt", .to = "missing_b.txt"}); It prints: missing_a.txt -> missing_b.txt The logger sees the calls of filesystem_t , not the calls of the queries . exists(filesystem, path) shows up as one STATUS . Note ABSOLUTE_PATH is not named ABSOLUTE , because wingdi.h defines a macro with that name. Faking and errors ¶ on_error and the logger belong to the filesystem that make_filesystem made. A fake that you write yourself has no logger and no handler: whatever it throws leaves the call. See Replacing calls in a test .

docs.text: Replacing calls in a test ¶ filesystem_t is a struct of std::function members. A test builds one and sets what the code under test needs. The code under test takes const filesystem_t& , so it works the same with the disk, a fake or a log. The code on this page is in the example/ directory of the library: config_loader.hpp , memory_filesystem.hpp and main.cpp . The code under test ¶ // true when dir has a regular file config.txt inline bool has_config( const virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t& filesystem, const virtual_filesystem::path_t& dir ) { return virtual_filesystem::is_regular_file(filesystem, dir / "config.txt"); } // the text of dir/config.txt, or an empty string when there is none inline std::string load_config( const virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t& filesystem, const virtual_filesystem::path_t& dir ) { return filesystem.try_read(dir / "config.txt").value_or(""); } Nothing here says where the files are. In the program you pass make_filesystem({}) . In a test you pass a fake. has_config ends in a call of status . What happens to that call depends on what the test put in status : The next sections show each case. A partial fake ¶ A default-constructed filesystem_t has every member empty. Set only the members that the code under test calls. has_config calls is_regular_file , which calls status , so one member is enough: namespace fs = std::filesystem; virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t& path) { return path == "dir/config.txt" ? fs::file_status{fs::file_type::regular} : fs::file_status{fs::file_type::not_found}; }; example::has_config(filesystem, "dir"); // true example::has_config(filesystem, "other"); // false The fake answers by path, so one fake covers many cases. Warning Calling an empty member throws std::bad_function_call . This is useful in a test: a call that you did not expect fails loudly instead of returning a made-up answer. virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t empty; empty.file_size("a"); // throws std::bad_function_call A fake that fails ¶ A fake can throw std::filesystem::filesystem_error , the exception that std::filesystem throws. The failure reaches the code under test the way a real one would: virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t denied; denied.status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t& path) -> fs::file_status { throw fs::filesystem_error{ "status", path, std::make_error_code(std::errc::permission_denied) }; }; example::has_config(denied, "dir"); // throws filesystem_error, path1() is "dir/config.txt" Without the library a test cannot make "permission denied" without a real file that is locked for the user. A filesystem that make_filesystem made catches errors of the real calls; it does not catch the exceptions of a fake that you set afterwards. See Errors and logging . Replace one member of a real filesystem ¶ make_filesystem returns an ordinary value. Replace a member of it when the rest should stay real: auto filesystem = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({}); filesystem.current_path = [] { return virtual_filesystem::path_t{"/work"}; }; filesystem.current_path(); // "/work", other members still use the disk A filesystem in memory ¶ When a test reads and writes files, one fake per call becomes long. memory_t of the example is a fake that keeps files in a std::map and fills seven members: status , file_size , create_directories , list , try_read , read and write . struct memory_t { std::map<virtual_filesystem::path_t, virtual_filesystem::bytes_t> files; virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem(); }; The members of filesystem() read and write files , so the memory_t must outlive the filesystem. Here is a piece of it, try_read and write : result.try_read = [this](const vfs::path_t& path) -> vfs::bytes_ot { const auto found = files.find(path); if (found == files.end()) { return {}; } return found->second; }; result.write = [this](const vfs::write_t& args) { files[args.path] = args.bytes; }; A test uses it with the code under test: example::memory_t memory; const auto filesystem = memory.filesystem(); example::load_config(filesystem, "dir"); // "": there is no file example::save_config(filesystem, "dir", "mode=fast"); // writes dir/config.txt example::load_config(filesystem, "dir"); // "mode=fast" example::has_config(filesystem, "dir"); // true filesystem.file_size("dir/config.txt"); // 9 You can look into memory.files to see what the code wrote, and fill it before the call to prepare input. Note memory_t is an example, not a part of the library. Directories are not stored. A memory filesystem for your tests should answer the calls your code makes and no more. What a fake should answer ¶ A fake replaces a call of std::filesystem , so it should answer the way std::filesystem does: status of a missing file is file_type::not_found . It is not an error. file_size of a missing file throws filesystem_error . try_read of a missing file is an empty optional. read of a missing file throws filesystem_error . The reference lists the result type of every member.

docs.text: filesystem_t is a struct of std::function members. A test builds one and sets what the code under test needs. The code under test takes const filesystem_t& , so it works the same with the disk, a fake or a log. The code on this page is in the example/ directory of the library: config_loader.hpp , memory_filesystem.hpp and main.cpp .
docs.title: Replacing calls in a test

docs.text: // true when dir has a regular file config.txt inline bool has_config( const virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t& filesystem, const virtual_filesystem::path_t& dir ) { return virtual_filesystem::is_regular_file(filesystem, dir / "config.txt"); } // the text of dir/config.txt, or an empty string when there is none inline std::string load_config( const virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t& filesystem, const virtual_filesystem::path_t& dir ) { return filesystem.try_read(dir / "config.txt").value_or(""); } Nothing here says where the files are. In the program you pass make_filesystem({}) . In a test you pass a fake. has_config ends in a call of status . What happens to that call depends on what the test put in status : The next sections show each case.
docs.title: The code under test

docs.text: A default-constructed filesystem_t has every member empty. Set only the members that the code under test calls. has_config calls is_regular_file , which calls status , so one member is enough: namespace fs = std::filesystem; virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t& path) { return path == "dir/config.txt" ? fs::file_status{fs::file_type::regular} : fs::file_status{fs::file_type::not_found}; }; example::has_config(filesystem, "dir"); // true example::has_config(filesystem, "other"); // false The fake answers by path, so one fake covers many cases. Warning Calling an empty member throws std::bad_function_call . This is useful in a test: a call that you did not expect fails loudly instead of returning a made-up answer. virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t empty; empty.file_size("a"); // throws std::bad_function_call
docs.title: A partial fake

docs.text: A fake can throw std::filesystem::filesystem_error , the exception that std::filesystem throws. The failure reaches the code under test the way a real one would: virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t denied; denied.status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t& path) -> fs::file_status { throw fs::filesystem_error{ "status", path, std::make_error_code(std::errc::permission_denied) }; }; example::has_config(denied, "dir"); // throws filesystem_error, path1() is "dir/config.txt" Without the library a test cannot make "permission denied" without a real file that is locked for the user. A filesystem that make_filesystem made catches errors of the real calls; it does not catch the exceptions of a fake that you set afterwards. See Errors and logging .

Getting started ¶ Requirements ¶ C++20. The library builds its arguments with designated initializers ( {.logger = ..., .on_error = ...} ), and the examples of this documentation use them everywhere. A compiler with std::filesystem : GCC, Clang and MSVC are tested. The library is a static library, not header-only: make_filesystem is in src/std_filesystem.cpp . The target is virtual_filesystem::virtual_filesystem . It carries the include directory and the C++20 requirement. CMake ¶ The library lives at github.com/goloveshin/virtual_filesystem . Fetch it with FetchContent : include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare( virtual_filesystem GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/goloveshin/virtual_filesystem.git GIT_TAG main ) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(virtual_filesystem) target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE virtual_filesystem::virtual_filesystem) Replace main with a release tag to pin a version. To use a local copy instead, replace GIT_REPOSITORY and GIT_TAG with SOURCE_DIR <path> . Include one header. The headers in detail are not included on their own: #include <virtual_filesystem/filesystem.hpp> The library has an option VIRTUAL_FILESYSTEM_BUILD_TESTS . It builds the unit tests and the example of the library. It is ON only when virtual_filesystem is the top-level project, so a project that uses the library does not build them. You can set it yourself before FetchContent_MakeAvailable : set(VIRTUAL_FILESYSTEM_BUILD_TESTS OFF) The first program ¶ #include <virtual_filesystem/filesystem.hpp> #include <iostream> namespace vfs = virtual_filesystem; namespace fs = std::filesystem; int main() { const auto filesystem = vfs::make_filesystem({ .logger = [](const vfs::log_t& log) { std::cout << "log: " << log.path.generic_string() << "
"; }, .on_error = [](const fs::filesystem_error& error) { std::cout << "error: " << error.path1().generic_string() << "
"; } }); const vfs::path_t path = "no_such_file.txt"; // a missing file is not an error for status const auto is_there = vfs::exists(filesystem, path); std::cout << std::boolalpha << "exists: " << is_there << "
"; // file_size of a missing file is an error: on_error runs, the result is 0 const auto size = filesystem.file_size(path); std::cout << "size: " << size << "
"; } It prints: log: no_such_file.txt exists: false log: no_such_file.txt error: no_such_file.txt size: 0 What happens here: make_filesystem returns a filesystem_t whose members call std::filesystem . The logger and on_error functions are held by every member. exists(filesystem, path) is a free function. It calls filesystem.status(path) , so the logger runs once. A missing file is file_type::not_found and not an error, so on_error does not run. filesystem.file_size(path) throws std::filesystem::filesystem_error in std::filesystem . Here the library catches it. The logger runs first, then on_error receives the error. Since on_error returns, the call returns 0 , a value-initialized std::uintmax_t . See Errors and logging . The example and the tests ¶ The example/ directory of the library has code under test, a filesystem in memory, and a program that checks how they work together. It builds and runs with the tests: cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure file what it is example/config_loader.hpp code under test: four functions that take a filesystem_t example/memory_filesystem.hpp memory_t , a fake that keeps files in a std::map example/main.cpp checks: fakes, queries, errors and logging, file bytes The pages of the guide quote this code.

docs.text: Listing a directory ¶ list returns the entries of a directory in one vector. It replaces both std::filesystem::directory_iterator and recursive_directory_iterator . struct list_options_t { bool recursive = false; bool follow_directory_symlink = false; bool skip_permission_denied = false; }; struct list_t { path_t root; list_options_t options = {}; }; using list_ft = std::function<entries_t (const list_t&)>; Arguments ¶ root is the directory. options selects how to walk it: option meaning recursive go into subdirectories. The default is the entries of root only follow_directory_symlink go into a symlink to a directory. It has an effect only with recursive skip_permission_denied skip a directory that cannot be opened, instead of an error The last two are std::filesystem::directory_options of the same names. The call takes one struct, so a call site names what it sets: const auto entries = filesystem.list({ .root = root, .options = {.recursive = true} }); The result ¶ struct entry_t { path_t path; fs::file_status status; fs::file_status symlink_status; }; using entries_t = std::vector<entry_t>; An entry is a snapshot . status and symlink_status are captured when the directory is listed, so the code that goes through the entries does not ask the filesystem again. In std::filesystem the same questions to directory_entry can touch the disk and can fail. status follows a symlink and symlink_status does not, the same as in the queries . The order of the entries is the order of the directory. It is not sorted. Sort the result when the order matters. Code under test ¶ source_files of the example takes the .cpp files under a root: inline std::vector<std::string> source_files( const virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t& filesystem, const virtual_filesystem::path_t& root ) { namespace fs = virtual_filesystem::fs; const auto entries = filesystem.list({ .root = root, .options = {.recursive = true} }); std::vector<std::string> result; for (const auto& entry : entries) { if (entry.status.type() == fs::file_type::regular && entry.path.extension() == ".cpp") { result.push_back(entry.path.generic_string()); } } std::ranges::sort(result); return result; } A fake list ¶ A test sets list and nothing else. The entries carry their own status, so no status fake is needed: virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.list = [](const virtual_filesystem::list_t& args) { const auto regular = fs::file_status{fs::file_type::regular}; return virtual_filesystem::entries_t{ {.path = args.root / "a.cpp", .status = regular, .symlink_status = regular}, {.path = args.root / "b.hpp", .status = regular, .symlink_status = regular}, {.path = args.root / "sub" / "c.cpp", .status = regular, .symlink_status = regular} }; }; example::source_files(filesystem, "src"); // {"src/a.cpp", "src/sub/c.cpp"} The memory filesystem of the example ( memory_t ) fills list from its files too, and honors recursive . See Replacing calls in a test . Errors ¶ If the directory cannot be opened or is not a directory, std::filesystem throws filesystem_error . With a filesystem from make_filesystem it goes to on_error , and the result is an empty vector: const auto filesystem = virtual_filesystem::make_filesystem({}); filesystem.list({.root = "missing_dir"}).size(); // 0 An error in the middle of a walk, for example a directory that cannot be opened without skip_permission_denied , also ends the call, and entries found before the error are not returned.

docs.text: Queries ¶ exists , is_regular_file , is_directory , is_empty , relative and the other questions that std::filesystem answers are free functions of the library. The first argument is the filesystem: virtual_filesystem::exists(filesystem, path); virtual_filesystem::is_directory(filesystem, path); virtual_filesystem::relative(filesystem, path, base); They are not members of filesystem_t , because they are rules. Each one is a few lines over the members, and it is the same for every filesystem: the disk: make_filesystem fills the members, the rules are the same; a fake: the test sets status , and exists answers from it. A fake cannot disagree with a rule, because the fake has no way to replace it. A test that says "this path is a directory" sets one status , and is_directory , exists , is_regular_file and is_other all follow. What each query reads ¶ query reads true when exists status the type is not none and not not_found is_regular_file status the type is regular is_directory status the type is directory is_block_file status the type is block is_character_file status the type is character is_fifo status the type is fifo is_socket status the type is socket is_other status the file exists and is not regular, not a directory and not a symlink is_symlink symlink_status the type is symlink is_empty status , then list or file_size a directory has no entries, or a file has size 0 relative weakly_canonical see below proximate weakly_canonical see below All of them are inline and take const filesystem_t& and const path_t& . A missing member that the query needs throws std::bad_function_call . status and symlink_status ¶ status follows a symlink and tells what the link points to. symlink_status does not follow it and tells what the link is. All the type queries except is_symlink use status : virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t&) { return fs::file_status{fs::file_type::regular}; }; filesystem.symlink_status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t&) { return fs::file_status{fs::file_type::symlink}; }; virtual_filesystem::is_regular_file(filesystem, "l"); // true: a link to a regular file virtual_filesystem::is_symlink(filesystem, "l"); // true: and it is a link This is one file and two answers, which is what a real symlink looks like. To build it on a disk you would need a user that is allowed to create symlinks. is_empty ¶ is_empty asks status first. A directory is empty when list({.root = path}) has no entries. The list is not recursive, and it is the call that a logger and a fake see. Anything else is empty when file_size(path) is 0. virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.status = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t&) { return fs::file_status{fs::file_type::directory}; }; filesystem.list = [](const virtual_filesystem::list_t&) { return virtual_filesystem::entries_t{}; }; virtual_filesystem::is_empty(filesystem, "d"); // true Warning A missing path is not a directory, so is_empty calls file_size . On a filesystem from make_filesystem that fails with filesystem_error ; if on_error returns, file_size returns 0 and is_empty answers true . Check exists first when "missing" must be different from "empty". relative and proximate ¶ Both make the two paths weakly canonical with the filesystem, and then cut the second from the first by their names only: // path relative to base path_t relative(const filesystem_t&, const path_t& path, const path_t& base); // path proximate to base: the path itself, when there is no relative path path_t proximate(const filesystem_t&, const path_t& path, const path_t& base); relative is lexically_relative of the canonical paths, proximate is lexically_proximate . virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.weakly_canonical = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t& path) { return path; }; relative(filesystem, "/a/b/c", "/a"); // "b/c" relative(filesystem, "/x/y", "/a"); // "../x/y" relative(filesystem, "x/y", "/a"); // "": a relative path and an absolute base have no relative path proximate(filesystem, "x/y", "/a"); // "x/y": the path itself The fake weakly_canonical returns the path as it is, so the test does not depend on the disk. On the disk the paths are resolved first: symlinks are followed and . and .. are removed, so two names of one place give one answer. Errors ¶ The queries do not catch anything. A member that throws filesystem_error makes the query throw it. With a filesystem from make_filesystem the member does not throw: it logs, calls on_error , and returns an empty result. See Errors and logging .

docs.text: Both make the two paths weakly canonical with the filesystem, and then cut the second from the first by their names only: // path relative to base path_t relative(const filesystem_t&, const path_t& path, const path_t& base); // path proximate to base: the path itself, when there is no relative path path_t proximate(const filesystem_t&, const path_t& path, const path_t& base); relative is lexically_relative of the canonical paths, proximate is lexically_proximate . virtual_filesystem::filesystem_t filesystem; filesystem.weakly_canonical = [](const virtual_filesystem::path_t& path) { return path; }; relative(filesystem, "/a/b/c", "/a"); // "b/c" relative(filesystem, "/x/y", "/a"); // "../x/y" relative(filesystem, "x/y", "/a"); // "": a relative path and an absolute base have no relative path proximate(filesystem, "x/y", "/a"); // "x/y": the path itself The fake weakly_canonical returns the path as it is, so the test does not depend on the disk. On the disk the paths are resolved first: symlinks are followed and . and .. are removed, so two names of one place give one answer.

docs.text: The queries do not catch anything. A member that throws filesystem_error makes the query throw it. With a filesystem from make_filesystem the member does not throw: it logs, calls on_error , and returns an empty result. See Errors and logging .
